title: The Butterfly Shares Computation
description: Set a, b and the twiddle angle W with sliders, toggle whether the b*W product is shared between both outputs, and compare the multiply/add instruction counts with and without sharing.
creator: Real-Time DSP on a $5 Microcontroller
author: Dan McCreary
subject: Digital Signal Processing
FFT
Algorithms

educational.topic: Why the FFT butterfly shares one multiplication between two outputs
learningObjectives: Compute both butterfly outputs from chosen a, b and twiddle angle W
Compare instruction counts for a butterfly that shares W*b against one that recomputes it
Explain why sharing one product between two outputs is the source of the FFT's saving
prerequisites: Twiddle factors on the unit circle

controls.label: Share b × W between both outputs

equations: with sharing: 4 real multiplies, 6 real adds
without sharing: 8 real multiplies, 8 real adds
assumptions: W lies on the unit circle at the chosen angle, matching a twiddle factor
"Without sharing" models recomputing the same W*b product independently for each output, as a direct DFT would
limitations: Shows one butterfly in isolation; stage assembly appears in later labs

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Analyze-level comparison with a live instruction-count readout
keyQuestions: How many real multiplies does sharing W*b save per butterfly?
How does that per-butterfly saving scale across a full FFT?
commonMisconceptions: That each butterfly output needs its own twiddle multiply
That the saving from the FFT comes from a faster multiply rather than doing fewer of them
assessmentOpportunities: Predict the savings percentage before toggling the checkbox
Scale the per-butterfly saving to the 2,304 butterflies in a 512-point FFT
